speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: asked the Minister for Law (a) whether there were similar instances of cheating by trainee lawyers in the years prior to the recent discovery of candidates cheating in the 2020 Part B Bar examination and (b) if so, what actions were taken against them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: asked the Minister for Law (a) whether any steps need to be taken to address public concerns about the law students found cheating; and (b) whether the punishments meted out are sufficient.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: asked the Minister for Law (a) whether the Singapore Institute of Legal Education (SILE) has observed a similar trend of trainee lawyers cheating in their Bar examinations, especially for the 2021 cohort; and (b) whether the Ministry intends to introduce any rules to regulate trainee lawyers' conduct so as to ensure that they are deemed ethically ready to be called to the Bar.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That would include Question Nos 3, 4 and 5 in the Order Paper from Mr Seah Kian Peng, Ms He Ting Ru and Ms Hany Soh, as well as Question No 11 for Written Answer from Mr Ang Wei Neng filed for today's Sitting.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, of course, the fact is that there is a difference between whether it has happened and what they have found.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It means that their applications to be admitted to the Bar will be heard at some time in the future, when the adjournments end.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To get admitted, they will need to convince all the stakeholders involved that they are fit and proper to practise law before they are allowed to do so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As with all admission applications, the High Court has the discretion to rule on whether a particular applicant should be admitted or should not be admitted, taking into account the views of the Attorney-General, SILE and the Law Society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We need to be careful about how much we discuss here and I have to be careful of what I say because the applications of the trainee lawyers who cheated are still pending in Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the circumstances, what I can say is this: lawyers are fiduciaries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are expected to act in the best interests of the clients they advise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are also officers of the Court, meaning they owe a very high duty to the Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have to be honest, both with their clients and with the Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have to act with the highest standards of probity to ensure that they can be relied upon with utmost confidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is not just as lawyers advising clients, but in every other aspect of their conduct.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Cheating is a serious derogation from the basic principle of honesty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think all this can be said without too much contention.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are levels of seriousness when lawyers behave dishonestly: misleading clients is serious, lying in Court is serious, lying on oath is serious.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is also other conduct which, if it is unbefitting of a lawyer, whether or not in the context of advising a client, can also be taken up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am sure Members, including the Members who have asked the questions, would accept that any such conduct is quite unacceptable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What happens to the particular trainee lawyers' applications, how they will be dealt with – the Courts will decide, taking into account the views of the respective institutions, which will put forward their views.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If you can keep it to two questions, please.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: First one: the Minister mentioned that SILE has since put in additional safeguards.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Of course, we could say we are smarter in hindsight, but my question is, why were some of these safeguards not put in place in the first instance?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: If some of the trainees in previous examinations – which is the question I filed – have subsequently been practising, may I ask the Minister whether the LawSoc has found any misconduct amongst any of them in that group?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Were there any similar cases of examinees that cheated in the past?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: My second supplementary question is: earlier on, we were concerned about second chances.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Given that the names of these candidates are now revealed, what can we say about giving them second chances?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Seah Kian Peng's first question is: why did SILE not put in safeguards earlier?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I assume that they, perhaps, expected lawyers to be more honest than what has turned out to be the case, at least, with regard to some of them; and, prior to COVID-19, examinations were usually conducted physically.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I do not think SILE has that much experience conducting it in this format.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, with regard to whether there were earlier cases, Sir, what I can say is: SILE says that it has not found situations of such cheating.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I drew a distinction between that and whether something like that has actually happened.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There was a second supplementary question, Minister, about second chances.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On whether it should be a question of second chances, I think the way we ought to approach it is this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The first point should be: what is the offence and who committed the offence?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You start with that and the message has got to go out to others that all of this will be dealt with very seriously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think anyone can dispute that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, at the same time, what is the right penalty?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I have said, that is before the Courts, so, we need to be careful.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think we can say this much.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Does that mean that we forever prevent them from practising?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think most people would think that is probably too harsh.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Should they face significant sanctions that bring across the seriousness of the conduct?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think most people would agree with that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Within that framework, how the Courts decide, I think we have to wait and see.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This question is akin to what Minister has just responded to, in relation to recommending having a rehabilitative nature or giving these trainee solicitors a second chance: whether we can also explore recommending that these trainee lawyers be conditionally called, continue to have close supervision by their supervising solicitors or representative from the Law Society and serve the community by volunteering in cases through the Legal Aid Bureau or the Criminal Legal Aid schemes, until they are deemed satisfied by their supervising solicitors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But these are not things that are decided by the Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We can decide as a matter of policy in future under the law, but for these specific cases, these are matters that are between the Attorney-General's Chambers and the Law Society to make suggestions and for the Courts to decide.
